paragraphs.text: Only 8 events are documented here, with 59 people and places; 5 of the 8 have approximate locations.
Sophocles was born here in 496 BCE and Pericles in 494 BCE, both at approximate locations.
In 480 BCE the Achaemenid Empire captured Athens, then razed the Acropolis, the Old Temple of Athena, and the Older Parthenon.
One year later, the Greek coalition retook Athens.
Socrates was born here in 470 BCE, placed approximately.
Pericles led Athens as its preeminent orator and statesman roughly from 461 to 429 BCE.
Aristophanes was born here in 445 BCE, also placed approximately.
Spartan invasions of Attica ran from 431 BCE to 425 BCE, and the Plague of Athens from 430 BCE to 426 BCE, both placed approximately.

cites.label: Spartan invasions of Attica during the Archidamian War

paragraphs.text: The plague killed an estimated 75,000 to 100,000 people, around 25% of the population.
Plato was born here between 429 BCE and 420 BCE, at an approximate location.
In 420 BCE an earthquake disrupted the Athenian assembly, also placed approximately.
In 404 BCE came the Siege of Athens.
At the Battle of Munichia, exiles under Thrasybulus held a hill in Piraeus, and the defeated Thirty Tyrants fled to Eleusis.
In 403 BCE, at the Battle of Piraeus, placed approximately, a Spartan force narrowly defeated the exiles, and a settlement then allowed the reestablishment of democratic government in Athens.
In 399 BCE Socrates was accused of impiety and corrupting the youth and sentenced to death.
The Athenian-Macedonian War followed from 340 BCE to 338 BCE, also placed approximately.
This account draws on the most notable of the 27 documented events here.
Ginkaku-ji, a Zen temple in Kyoto's Sakyo ward, is dated to 1465.
The Ōnin War, a civil war from 1467 to 1477, grew from a dispute between Hosokawa Katsumoto and Yamana Sōzen.
The Battle of Goryō is recorded here in 1467.
After that war weakened the Ashikaga shogunate, local samurai and peasants in Yamashiro Province rose up in 1485 and demanded the withdrawal of two rival warlord armies.
Their league, placed only approximately, operated until 1493, when a new invasion forced its members to reaccept the shogunate's authority.
The Eiroku Incident, a 1565 battle, has an approximate location, and the Battle of Yasugawara is recorded in 1570.
In 1571 Oda Nobunaga fought the sōhei of Enryaku-ji on Mount Hiei near Kyoto.
The Siege of Makishima Castle, a 1573 battle, is also placed approximately.
In 1582 Nobunaga died by seppuku at Honnō-ji in Kyoto in the rebellion of his vassal Akechi Mitsuhide.
The Battle of Yamazaki, between the forces of Akechi Mitsuhide and Toyotomi Hideyoshi, was fought in 1582.
Emperor Go-Mizunoo was born here in 1596, at an approximate location.
In 1600 Fushimi Castle, defended by Torii Mototada for Tokugawa Ieyasu, fell in a battle leading up to the decisive Battle of Sekigahara.
That year Kyōgoku Takatsugu held Ōtsu castle for the Tokugawa.
Empress Meishō was born here in 1624, Go-Kōmyō in 1633 and Go-Sai in 1638, all at approximate locations.
Only 3 events and 1 place are documented here, so this account is short.
The First Battle of Panipat, on 21 April 1526, was fought between the invading forces of Babur and Ibrahim Khan Lodi, the Sultan of Delhi.
Babur's forces, employing gunpowder firearms and cannons, defeated Ibrahim in one of the earliest battles involving gunpowder arms on the Indian subcontinent.
The victory marked the beginning of Mughal rule in India.
The Kabuli Bagh Mosque in Panipat was built in 1527 by the emperor Babur to mark that victory, and it is named after Kabuli Begum, Babur's wife.

cites.label: Kabuli Bagh Mosque with enclosure wall

paragraphs.text: The Second Battle of Panipat was fought on 5 November 1556, between the Mughals under Akbar and king Hemu, titularly known as Hemchandra Vikramaditya.
A few weeks earlier, Hemchandra had conquered Delhi and Agra by defeating Mughal forces under Tardi Beg Khan in the Battle of Delhi.
The Third Battle of Panipat took place on 14 January 1761, in and around the city of Panipat, between the Maratha Empire and the invading army of the Durrani Empire.
The Afghans were supported by three key allies in India: Najib-ud-Daula, elements of the declining Mughal Empire, and the Oudh State under Shuja-ud-Daula.
The Maratha army was led by Sadashivrao Bhau, third-highest authority of the Maratha Confederacy after the Chhatrapati and the Peshwa.
